newsitem.title: IRAN: Profiles of Iran's four election candidates.
newsitem.headline: Profiles of Iran's four election candidates.

text.p: Four candidates are standing in next Friday's election to succeed President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who must step down in August after eight years in office.
Here are brief profiles of them:
Mohammad Khatami, 54, is a former minister of culture and Islamic guidance known for advocating less heavy-handed social and cultural policies and regulations.
He is backed by a coalition of centrists close to Rafsanjani and Islamist left-wingers who have moderated many of their views in recent years.
A Shi'ite Moslem clergyman, he wears a black turban and is referred to deferentially by the honorific Seyed, signs that he commands special respect as a descendant from Prophet Mohammad.

Khatami has a reputation as a tolerant politician and has gained wide support among women, young people and intellectuals who fear a harder application of Islamic mores in everyday life and restrictions on freedom of expression.

Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, 54, is speaker of the Majlis (parliament) and leader of a conservative group of Shi'ite Moslem clergymen who together with their allies have a majority in the 270-seat assembly.

He has been backed by key clerical groups and is close to the bazaaris, traders who make up Iran's traditional merchant class and who fear their economic and political advantage are threatened by foreign investment in the economy.
Conservative deputies have slowed Rafsanjani's market reforms but Nateq-Nouri's supporters now say he would push ahead with them if elected.
A clergyman's son, he was interior minister from December 1981 to August 1985 when he left the cabinet over political differences.

Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri, 51, was a revolutionary court judge. He became revolutionary Iran's first intelligence (internal security) minister from 1984 to 1989. He was prosecutor general from 1989 to 1993, when he was put in charge of Iranian Moslems' annual haj pilgrimage to Islamic holy sites in Saudi Arabia.
He has memorised the entire Islamic holy book, the Koran.
A fierce defender of Islamic values, he is known for his hardline conservative views and has advocated closer adherence to the principles of the 1979 revolution.

In comments published in a Persian daily earlier this month he said the death edict imposed by Iran's revolutionary leader the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini in 1989 on British author Salman Rushdie for blaspheming Islam in his book "The Satanic Verses" is still in force and should be carried out.
Reza Zavarei, 59, is a lawyer who is deputy head of the judiciary and he has also been in charge of the real estate and documents registration organisation since 1989.

Prosecutor of the Islamic Revolution Court in Tehran and deputy interior minister after the 1979 revolution, he was a Tehran deputy in the Majlis (parliament) for two terms. Like the other candidates he is a Shi'ite Moslem but he is the only one of the four who is not a cleric.
Prior to the revolution he was arrested and imprisoned twice for political activities.

Newspapers have noted he belongs to the same political faction as Nateq-Nouri and so could split the conservative vote, allowing Khatami to win without a run-off. Or he could take votes both from Khatami and Reyshahri and give them to Nateq- Nouri in a second round.
